How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • In a recent development, “Congratulations!
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which stated something like,.

In a recent development, “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

According to recent reports, during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

According to recent reports, but eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Industry observers note that admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It has been revealed that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

Recent findings suggest that it reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Sources indicate that experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning newly introduced things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

It has been revealed that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

It has been revealed that but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

It has been revealed that we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

*(Vine Gold is not all that useful as it turns out as 99.9% of the available items seem to be the same trinkets you see in the Silver tier).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if your pet eats the same food month after month, buy it on autoship. On eligible items, the big pet retailers take 35% off the first order, up to $20, and 5% off every one after. Set the delivery interval to how long a bag lasts, and check the price before each order ships.

Say your dog goes through a $70 bag of food every month and the price holds all year. At 5% off, autoship saves $3.50 on each bag, or $42 a year.

Sources indicate that chewy, Petco, and PetSmart all run autoship the same basic way. On eligible items, each takes 35% off your first autoship order, up to $20, then 5% off every order after that, and each offers free shipping on orders over $49. You can cancel anytime, and skip or reschedule a delivery until a day or two before it’s processed.

Sources indicate that make your first autoship order about $57 or more, the point where 35% off reaches the $20 cap. In the example above, the first bag saves $20 instead of $3.50, which brings the first year’s savings to $58.50. If the food alone comes in under $57, add litter, treats, or your pet’s monthly preventives to the order. Chewy and Petco ship prescription items on autoship too, once your vet verifies the prescription.

Each order is charged at the item’s current price, not the price you signed up at. All three stores email you before an order goes out, so check the price then, and skip or delay the delivery when the price has jumped or the current bag is still half full. Now and then, compare the autoship price with a sale elsewhere or a warehouse club’s price, since 5% off a $70 bag is only $3.50.

Start autoship the week your current bag runs low, since Chewy and Petco ship the first order right away. Then write the date on each upcoming bag you open, and set the interval to the number of days it lasts.

Close the gap that appears most often, with your employer paying if it will, and add the new skill to your resume and LinkedIn profile.

Sources indicate that skills go stale faster than most people notice. The World Economic Forum surveyed more than 1,000 large employers worldwide for its latest Future of Jobs Report, which projects that, on average, 39% of workers’ existing skills will change or go out of date by 2030.

One posting is a wish list, but a skill that turns up in most of 15 postings is a requirement. The postings for the job a step above yours show what it takes to get promoted.

Industry observers note that search your job title on Indeed or LinkedIn, then the title one step up, and open 10 to 20 current postings. Write down every skill, software program, and certification they ask for, and add a tally mark each time one repeats. The most-tallied item you don’t have yet is the gap to close first.

Industry observers note that if your applications keep stalling after graduation, run the same count on entry-level postings. A requirement that keeps showing up in postings but not on your resume could be what’s holding your applications back.

According to recent reports, close the gap the cheapest way that works. Ask your manager whether your employer’s training budget will cover a course, or take a low-cost online course on your own. You can also volunteer for a stretch assignment, a project just beyond your current role that puts the skill to use. Say a bookkeeper finds a payroll certification in most postings one step up, and one accounting software package in nearly as many. She starts with the certification and asks her manager to pay for the course, since it helps with the payroll work her team already does.

Then make the upcoming skill visible to the people who decide whether you get hired or promoted. List it on your resume in the postings’ own words, add it to your LinkedIn profile, and bring one result from using it to your next performance review.

Stocks Have Fallen About 30% Around Recessions – but Usually Bottomed Before They Ended

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The S&P 500’s largest drop around a recession has averaged about 30% since 1948, but the index has usually hit bottom before the recession ended.
  • Selling when a recession is declared often means selling after the worst is over.
  • Industry observers note that that 30% average is our count across the 12 recessions since 1948, from Yardeni Research’s record of S&P 500 declines and the NBER’s recession dates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The S&P 500’s largest drop around a recession has averaged about 30% since 1948, but the index has usually hit bottom before the recession ended. So don’t sell because one is coming or has just been declared. Keep money you’ll need within five years out of stocks beforehand, and keep investing on schedule through the downturn.

Selling when a recession is declared often means selling after the worst is over. The National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), which dates U.S. recessions, declared three of the last six recessions only after the S&P 500 had hit bottom.

Industry observers note that that 30% average is our count across the 12 recessions since 1948, from Yardeni Research’s record of S&P 500 declines and the NBER’s recession dates. In four of them, the drop stayed under 20%. The worst, 57% from October 2007 to March 2009, came with a financial crisis. Economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff found that severe financial crises bring deep, long slumps in stock prices, output, and employment.

The S&P 500 usually peaked before a recession began. It hit bottom before the recession ended in 11 of the 12, most often three to six months before. The exception was 2001, when stocks didn’t hit bottom until October 2002, almost a year after that recession ended. In 2009, the low came on March 9, three months before the recession ended in June. An investor who sold and waited for the recession to end would usually have bought back after stocks had already started to rise.

So prepare before a recession starts. Move money you’ll need within five years out of stocks and into a high-yield savings account, so a 30% drop can’t force you to sell low when you need the cash.

Industry observers note that once a recession starts, keep investing on schedule, and leave your 401(k) contributions and any automatic investments running even after it’s declared. The S&P 500 rose in the year after 11 of the 12 recessions ended, dividends included, by First Trust’s count.

At the bottom of a 30% drop, each $500 you invest buys about 43% more shares of an S&P 500 index fund than it did at the peak.

  • USDA’s latest estimates, for fiscal 2022, show nearly half of eligible people in households above the poverty line going without SNAP.
  • Sources indicate that to qualify, your household’s gross monthly income, meaning pay and other income before taxes, must stay under 130% of the federal poverty line for its size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your income has dropped or your pay no longer lasts the month, check whether you qualify for SNAP, the grocery benefit once called food stamps, before deciding you earn too much. Apply through your state’s SNAP office right away, since approved benefits count back to the day you apply.

USDA’s latest estimates, for fiscal 2022, show nearly half of eligible people in households above the poverty line going without SNAP.

Sources indicate that to qualify, your household’s gross monthly income, meaning pay and other income before taxes, must stay under 130% of the federal poverty line for its size. USDA’s limit for a household of four in the lower 48 states or D.C. is $3,575. USDA’s chart of state rules highlights 27 states and D.C. raising that limit to 200% of the poverty line and most states dropping the federal $3,000 cap on savings. A household with someone 60 or older or disabled skips the gross income test, and its federal savings cap is $4,750.

In the lower 48 states or D.C., a family of four with $2,800 a month in pay and no other income would get about $420 a month, more with high rent or child care costs and less as pay rises. The maximum there for a family of four is $1,023.

Apply through your state’s SNAP office, online where it’s offered or at a local office, and expect an interview. Bring pay stubs and your rent and utility bills as proof. The office has 30 days to decide, but a household with under $150 in monthly gross income and under $100 in cash and bank accounts can get benefits within 7 days.

In a recent development, pregnant women, new mothers, and children under 5 can also qualify for food benefits from WIC. For rent and utilities, look into emergency help with those bills.

Recent findings suggest that adults 18 to 64 with no child under 14 at home must work, train, or volunteer 80 hours a month to keep SNAP past three months in three years, unless they’re pregnant, unable to work, or otherwise exempt. Since 2025, that rule also covers veterans and homeless adults. Report income changes as your state directs, since you must repay any overpayment.

It has been revealed that turn in the application right away with your name, address, phone number, and signature. The office accepts it that day, and a SNAP worker helps you finish the rest at the interview.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That remarked, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like newly introduced credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most crucial issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Sources indicate that most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

It has been revealed that in fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That noted, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

Recent findings suggest that there are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an glitch with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

In a recent development, college students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that leading economic indicators such as the yield curve tend to turn months or even years before a recession, and sometimes no recession follows.
  • The Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index, which combines 10 such indicators, went nearly two years without a monthly gain after February 2022, and no recession began in that time.
  • Recent findings suggest that leading indicators shift before the wider economy does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that leading economic indicators such as the yield curve tend to turn months or even years before a recession, and sometimes no recession follows. When one flashes, don’t sell your stocks on it. Use the warning as a prompt to check your emergency fund, your plan for a job loss, and your mix of stocks and bonds.

The Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index, which combines 10 such indicators, went nearly two years without a monthly gain after February 2022, and no recession began in that time. A warning that can run two years and still be wrong can’t tell you when to sell.

Recent findings suggest that leading indicators shift before the wider economy does. Lagging ones, such as the unemployment rate, keep moving after the economy turns. The most quoted leading ones include:.

The yield curve’s record has the same catch. It inverted 6 to 24 months before each of the nine U.S. recessions from 1955 to 2018, the San Francisco Fed found, and a mid-1960s inversion brought a slowdown but no official recession. Measured as the gap between 10-year and 3-month Treasury rates, it inverted in October 2022 and stayed that way until December 2024, the St. Louis Fed’s data show, and no recession began in that time. Anyone who sold stocks when it inverted missed a rise of about 57% in the S&P 500 stock index by the time it flipped back, not counting dividends.

It has been revealed that so instead of selling, use the warning to check three things. Your emergency fund should cover three to six months of bare-bones bills. Your job-loss plan should list the costs you’d cut first and how soon to file for unemployment. And your mix of stocks and bonds should leave out money you’ll need within about five years, which belongs in savings.

Start with the emergency fund, since it helps whether or not a recession comes. An automatic transfer from each paycheck to savings builds it without selling anything.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Sources indicate that printers show how far apart the two totals can get. Take a $100 cartridge inkjet and a $240 ink-tank printer you refill from bottles, both from the same maker at full price.

So once the inkjet’s starter cartridges run out, the cartridges you buy cost more than the $140 you saved on the printer within about 1,500 pages of text. That’s two and a half years at 50 pages a month, or 12 and a half years at 10.

To compare any two models, total each one over the years you’ll keep it:.

According to recent reports, these totals assume both models last as long as you’ll keep them, and how long each one lasts decides whether buying the cheapest option saves money.   • Small, visible projects lead the list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most home improvements add less to your sale price than they cost, and the bigger the project, the less of its cost you get back. Remodel for your own use, and if you’ll sell within a few years, pick small, visible projects like a newly introduced garage door or entry door, which recoup the most.

In a recent development, zonda’s 2025 Cost vs. Value report compares the average cost of 28 common remodeling projects with what each adds to a home’s sale price. By its national averages, only five added more than they cost, and each of those cost less than $30,000.

Small, visible projects lead the list. A upcoming garage door cost an average $4,672 and added an estimated $12,507, and a steel entry door averaged $2,435 and added $5,270. Manufactured stone veneer on the lower front of the house and fiber-cement siding also paid for themselves. So did a midrange minor kitchen remodel, which keeps the cabinet boxes but replaces the doors, counters, and appliances.

Big projects sit near the bottom. A midrange primary suite addition averaged $170,517 and recouped 32% of its cost, an upscale major kitchen remodel 36%, and an upscale suite addition 18%. A buyer pays for what most buyers want, and a big remodel is built to one owner’s taste. So remodel for the years you’ll live in the house, and choose projects for resale only when a sale is near.

Planning to sell within three years? By those averages, a upcoming garage door and steel entry door would cost about $7,100 together and add about $17,800, so you’d come out about $10,700 ahead. The midrange suite addition would add about $55,100 for its $170,517 and leave you about $115,400 behind.

It has been revealed that before any upgrade, keep the roof, furnace, plumbing, and wiring sound and up to code. A buyer’s inspection will turn up a failing one, and you’ll pay to fix it or take a lower offer. Keep a kitchen or bath in line with the houses around you, too. A midrange bath remodel recouped 80% of its $26,138 average cost, and an upscale one 42% of $81,612.

Favor energy upgrades that pay for themselves in lower bills, since solar panels recouped just 30% of their $55,937 average cost at sale.

Buyers judge a remodel by its condition, not its cost, so a kitchen redone 10 years before you list is priced as a 10-year-old kitchen.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

If an hour of his time is worth more than $29, hiring beats doing the work himself, provided he can cover the $500 yearly loss.

If your hours are worth more than the manager’s cost per hour, vet each management firm before you sign.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

Industry observers note that these popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

Industry observers note that my goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

In a recent development, when it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

It has been revealed that the most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

Sources indicate that true Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

It has been revealed that one of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

Industry observers note that the program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

In a recent development, true Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Sources indicate that dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive proposal for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

It has been revealed that while Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

Sources indicate that the teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

Recent findings suggest that moneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

In a recent development, moneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

In a recent development, for those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Industry observers note that ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive proposal to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. Breaking: My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

According to recent reports, I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

In a recent development, but a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

Recent findings suggest that yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

Industry observers note that so I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s upcoming firm, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

Industry observers note that the next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

In a recent development, this is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

It has been revealed that but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

According to recent reports, many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

Recent findings suggest that so I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty swiftly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Recent findings suggest that many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term looks again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the problem, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

Recent findings suggest that and it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

Industry observers note that the great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The manufacturer that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Recent findings suggest that note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

Sources indicate that I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

In the Comments: Do you have questions about hormone replacement or anything else in this article? I’ll try to invite Kevin, Dr. Sean Bender and other knowledgeable people to contribute and answer questions as well.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re married, file your taxes jointly unless separate returns save you more than they cost.
  • According to recent reports, keeping separate bank accounts doesn’t call for separate tax returns.
  • Separate filers can’t claim the education credits or the student loan interest deduction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re married, file your taxes jointly unless separate returns save you more than they cost. Filing separately gives up several credits and deductions, but it can win when one of you has major medical bills or an income-driven student loan payment. Prepare your return both ways before you file.

According to recent reports, keeping separate bank accounts doesn’t call for separate tax returns. File jointly by default, since the IRS says separate returns generally cost a couple more combined tax.

Separate filers can’t claim the education credits or the student loan interest deduction. Couples who live together also lose the earned income and child care credits. Through 2028, the new deductions for tips, overtime, and seniors require a joint return too. If one of you itemizes deductions, the other loses the standard deduction.

Spouses who lived apart for the last six months of the year should check which filing status they qualify for first. In a community property state, separate returns split your combined earnings in half.

According to recent reports, two situations can still make separate returns cheaper. One is significant medical bills for the spouse with the lower income. Itemized medical costs are deductible only above 7.50% of adjusted gross income, and a separate return applies that threshold to one income instead of two. Only bills that spouse paid count, and the deduction must outweigh what separate returns give up.

Sources indicate that the other is an income-driven student loan plan, which generally counts only the borrower’s income when you file separately. Say only you have student loans, repaid on the Repayment Assistance Plan. Your adjusted gross income is $36,000, your spouse’s is $32,000, and you have no kids. A joint return sets your payment at 6% of $68,000, or $4,080 a year, and a separate one at 3% of $36,000, or $1,080. Filing separately wins unless it adds more than $3,000 to your tax.

Separate returns also protect you from a spouse’s tax problems. On a joint return, either of you can owe all of its tax, interest, and penalties, even on income only one of you earned, so doubts about your spouse’s return can justify filing separately.

Settle the choice before the due date. After that, a joint return can’t be changed to separate ones, though separate returns can generally be amended into a joint return for up to three years.

Split Bills by Income When One Partner Earns Much More – Keep Fun Money Equal

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when one of you earns far more, split shared bills in proportion to take-home pay instead of 50/50, and give each of you the same personal spending money, no questions asked.
  • A 50/50 split looks fair until your incomes are far apart.
  • Having the higher earner cover everything removes that strain, but it can give that partner more say over how the household’s money gets spent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when one of you earns far more, split shared bills in proportion to take-home pay instead of 50/50, and give each of you the same personal spending money, no questions asked. Then protect the lower earner by deciding big purchases together and saving for retirement in both names.

A 50/50 split looks fair until your incomes are far apart. If one of you takes home $7,000 a month and the other $3,000, splitting $5,000 in shared bills down the middle takes about 36% of the higher earner’s pay and 83% of the lower earner’s.

Having the higher earner cover everything removes that strain, but it can give that partner more say over how the household’s money gets spent. A split by income avoids both problems, since each of you puts the same share of your own pay toward the bills. Here that’s 70% and 30% of the $5,000, or $3,500 and $1,500, which is half of each partner’s take-home pay.

On its own, the split still leaves each of you the other half of your pay, $3,500 for the higher earner against $1,500 for the lower earner. So each of you keeps the same allowance of fun money, say $300 a month, to spend without explaining it, and what’s left, $3,200 and $1,200 here, goes to savings goals you set together.

According to recent reports, to find your own split, divide each partner’s take-home pay by your combined total. Each of you then pays your share into a joint account for shared bills on payday. The same split works when one of you cuts back to care for kids. The bigger paycheck covers most or all of the bills, and the equal allowance means the partner who cut back never has to ask for spending money.

According to recent reports, then protect the partner who earns less. Make any purchase over an agreed amount, say $500, a joint decision, even when the higher earner pays for it. Keep retirement saving going in both names. If you’re married and file jointly, a spousal IRA lets one paycheck fund an individual retirement account for each of you. And buy term life insurance on the higher earner’s life, since losing that income would cut your household’s take-home pay by 70% here.

Rerun the percentages the month either take-home pay changes, whether from a raise, a new job, or a move to part-time hours.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Treat lottery tickets as entertainment you pay for, never as a plan to get ahead.
  • A record jackpot can make a few extra tickets feel like a smart move.
  • Industry observers note that those odds are 1 in 292.2 million for a $2 Powerball play and 1 in 290.5 million for a $5 Mega Millions play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Treat lottery tickets as entertainment you pay for, never as a plan to get ahead. On average, states pay out about 67 cents in prizes for every dollar of tickets sold, and the Powerball jackpot is a 1-in-292-million shot. Set a monthly limit near what a night out costs you, and stop once it’s spent.

A record jackpot can make a few extra tickets feel like a smart move. Each ticket’s odds stay the same, though, however massive the prize grows.

Industry observers note that those odds are 1 in 292.2 million for a $2 Powerball play and 1 in 290.5 million for a $5 Mega Millions play. Across all lottery games, states sold $104.7 billion in tickets in fiscal 2024 and paid out $70.2 billion in prizes, the Census Bureau reports. Players as a group lost about a third of what they spent. That loss is a fair price for a few days of daydreaming, but it rules tickets out as a way to build wealth.

In a recent development, in a national survey for a National Bureau of Economic Research study, lottery spending fell only modestly as income rose. That means lower-income households spend a bigger share of what they earn on tickets than higher earners do. Pay for your tickets only with money left after bills and savings.

It has been revealed that A $20-a-week habit costs $1,040 a year. Invest that $1,040 at the end of each year for 20 years instead, at an assumed 7% annual return, and you’d have about $42,600, more than double the $20,800 you put in. Keep the ticket budget small, and save or invest what you’d have spent beyond it.

If you enjoy playing, these steps keep the thrill and limit what it costs.

Count every ticket as money spent the moment you buy it, since about 24 of every 25 Powerball plays win nothing at all.

According to recent reports, karma keeps the items you save from any online store in one list and also warns you when one is about to sell out. Its browser extension and app apply coupon codes at checkout, too, and earn you cash back at partner stores such as Levi’s, Chanel, and Adidas.

Breaking: Passing the 1% Rule Isn’t Enough – Check a Rental’s Cash Flow Before You Offer

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that run a rental’s numbers yourself before you offer: what it nets each month after every expense and the mortgage, what you earn on the cash you put in, and how well its income covers the loan.
  • A rental can pass the 1% rule and still leave you almost nothing each month.
  • Sources indicate that say a $210,000 house rents for $2,100, exactly 1% of its price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that run a rental’s numbers yourself before you offer: what it nets each month after every expense and the mortgage, what you earn on the cash you put in, and how well its income covers the loan. The 1% rule, monthly rent at 1% of the price, only tells you which listings deserve that math.

A rental can pass the 1% rule and still leave you almost nothing each month. A listing’s projected return uses someone else’s assumptions, not yours.

Sources indicate that say a $210,000 house rents for $2,100, exactly 1% of its price. Taxes, insurance, repairs, savings for big replacements like a roof, and rent lost to empty months come to $9,600 a year. You put down 20%, or $42,000, pay $6,000 in closing costs, and borrow the other $168,000 on a 30-year investment-property loan at 8%.

A year’s rent minus every cost but the mortgage is the net operating income, here $15,600. Divide it by the price for the cap rate, 7.4%. The $1,233 monthly loan payment leaves $67 a month of cash flow, or $807 a year, which is a 1.7% cash-on-cash return on the $48,000 you put in. Many lenders check a version of the debt service coverage ratio, net operating income divided by a year of loan payments, and here it’s 1.05, barely above the 1.0 at which the income just covers the loan. Pay a property manager 8% of the rent, and you lose $101 a month.

Before you offer, swap each of the listing’s assumptions for your own:.

According to recent reports, compare your total with the 50% rule, which puts every cost but the mortgage at about half the rent. A total far below half the rent is a sign you missed a cost.

Last, rerun the cash flow with an extra month empty, with rent 10% lower, and with a new roof in year one. Offer no more than the price at which the cash flow stays above zero in the first two cases, and keep enough cash on hand to replace the roof.

  • Every extra splash of detergent or squeeze of shampoo is product you paid for and then rinsed down the drain.
  • Industry observers note that the dose on a detergent label is set for typical wash conditions and gives the best cleaning, indicates the American Cleaning Institute, the trade group for cleaning-product makers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, pour laundry detergent to the fill line your label gives for your load size, not to the brim of the cap, and the same jug lasts for more loads. In the bathroom, use a small dab of shampoo, a pea-size bit of toothpaste, and a foaming pump filled with soap thinned with water.

Every extra splash of detergent or squeeze of shampoo is product you paid for and then rinsed down the drain.

Industry observers note that the dose on a detergent label is set for typical wash conditions and gives the best cleaning, indicates the American Cleaning Institute, the trade group for cleaning-product makers. Pour past it for an ordinary load and the jug just empties sooner. Too much detergent can even leave residue on your clothes, Whirlpool says.

Say your jug’s label promises 64 loads at the medium-load line, and you’ve been pouring 50% more than that each time. The jug runs out after about 43 loads. Pour to the line and you get all 64 loads instead of 43, about 50% more, so two jugs now do the work of three.

In a recent development, start with the fill line for your load size, using a high-efficiency (HE) detergent if your washer is an HE model. Then use less for a small or lightly soiled load or soft water, and more for a large or heavily soiled load or hard water (water high in minerals), as the institute advises.

The same goes for the bathroom shelf.

Before your next load, find the fill line your detergent’s label gives for the load you wash most, and pour to it every time.

Buy a Rental for Its Cash Flow – Treat Price Gains as a Bonus

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A rental that loses money each month is a bet that home prices will rise, and when they stall or fall, you keep covering the shortfall or sell at a loss.
  • Industry observers note that picture an investor who bought a condo in 2006 expecting price gains of 10% a year to make up for rent that fell $1,000 a month short of its costs.
  • A rental with negative cash flow, meaning rent that falls short of its costs, pays off only if prices climb fast enough to cover the shortfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A rental that loses money each month is a bet that home prices will rise, and when they stall or fall, you keep covering the shortfall or sell at a loss. Buy one whose rent covers every cost, from the mortgage to repairs and vacancies, and treat any rise in value as extra.

Industry observers note that picture an investor who bought a condo in 2006 expecting price gains of 10% a year to make up for rent that fell $1,000 a month short of its costs. By 2011 the condo was worth 30% less, and the investor sold at a loss after paying $60,000 to cover five years of shortfalls.

A rental with negative cash flow, meaning rent that falls short of its costs, pays off only if prices climb fast enough to cover the shortfall. Every repair and every vacancy adds to the shortfall, and borrowing makes a price drop worse. With 20% down, a 20% fall in price wipes out your whole down payment, because the loan doesn’t shrink when the price does.

The Federal Housing Finance Agency’s national index of home prices fell nearly 20% from its April 2007 peak by March 2011. In Austin, Texas, home prices jumped nearly 60% from 2020 to 2022, then the median price fell 22% from its pandemic peak by mid-2025, the Texas Real Estate Research Center found. Over the long run, most of what houses earned came from rent. In a typical year from 1890 to 2006, a house returned about 9% after inflation, with 7.7% from rent, before expenses, and only 1.3% from rising prices, a Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia working paper found.

Sources indicate that so buy only a property whose rent covers the mortgage, taxes, insurance, and a budget for repairs and vacancies. In an expensive market, that may mean buying in a city where rent still covers a mortgage. Run the full numbers before you make an offer. If the rent falls short, put more down to shrink the payment, or wait for a property that pays its own way.

Count the loan balance you pay down each month, and any rise in value, as your long-run gain, not as money toward the monthly costs.

You can hold a rental that covers its own costs through a slump, because the rent, not your paycheck, keeps paying the loan.
